scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm being AITA (A Guy in Trouble) for refusing to pump my girlfriend's tire. Let me start by understanding the situation better. From what I gather, whenever my girlfriend has any car maintenance issues, she tends to hold me accountable for fixing them or taking care of it. I noticed one of her tires was low and warned her about it before she left for work. A day later, the tire was completely flat because she didn't pump air into it or get it inspected. I ended up fixing it for her and even bought her a PSI gauge to help her monitor the tire pressure. I also noticed a pattern where she kept asking me to handle other car-related tasks. I made it clear that I don't know much about fixing cars beyond the basics like changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, and jump-starting. She insisted that I call her dad or watch YouTube videos to learn more, but I preferred that a mechanic handle it and suggested she learn how to do these things herself. Now, another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two. She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive to the gas station to fill the tire as needed until she gets it fixed or replaced. She claims she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. I asked her why she needed strangers (who are always men) to do something I've already taught her how to do. She said she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately, it's a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner, regardless of gender, she should know how to do something as basic as pumping a tire and changing a flat, especially since I showed her how. I mentioned that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in Distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and might need to know how to do these things instead of relying on strangers. She replied that all her male friends and family agreed with her and that they were "real men" because they knew how to take care of a woman. I don't really care for these outdated gender roles and have made that clear. On top of that, I do plenty of handywork around the house, cook and clean regularly (I cook more often than she does), and pay the majority of our expenses, including her rent. I don't see how this makes me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards or stereotype expectations just because she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused. Now, I'm determined not to lift a finger. Am I being AITA here? Alright, so I need to break this down. First, I should consider the dynamics of the relationship. It seems like there's a pattern where she expects me to handle all her car maintenance issues, even though I've made it clear that I don't have expertise beyond the basics. She also seems to have traditional views about gender roles, expecting men to take care of things like car repairs, while she doesn't want to get involved or learn how to do it herself. I, on the other hand, have a more modern perspective, believing that both partners should share responsibilities and that she should learn to handle basic car maintenance. I've even taken steps to help her by buying her a PSI gauge and offering to teach her how to use the pump. However, she's resistant to learning and insists on relying on strangers or expecting me to handle it. I also mentioned that I handle a lot of other responsibilities around the house, like cooking, cleaning, and paying the majority of the expenses. This adds to the imbalance in the relationship, where I'm taking on more responsibilities than her, but she still expects me to handle her car issues. Now, I'm at a point where I'm determined not to lift a finger regarding her tire issue. I want to know if this is AITA. To determine that, I need to consider whether my actions are fair, reasonable, and respectful in the context of our relationship. First, let's look at the expectations. She expects me to handle her car maintenance, but I've already shown willingness to help by fixing the tire, buying her tools, and offering to teach her. However, she's not willing to take responsibility or learn, which creates a cycle where I'm constantly being called upon to fix her car issues. On the other hand, I'm handling a significant portion of the household responsibilities, which might make me feel overburdened. It's reasonable to feel that way, especially if I'm already contributing a lot and she's not reciprocating in areas where she could take on more responsibility. Now, is it AITA to refuse to help with her tire? Well, AITA typically refers to situations where a man is being overly accommodating or enabling behavior that's unhealthy or unfair. In this case, it seems more like I'm setting boundaries to prevent being taken advantage of. However, I should also consider the impact on our relationship. If I stop helping with her car issues, she might feel unsupported or even more frustrated. It could lead to arguments or tension. On the other hand, if I continue to help without her taking responsibility, I might feel resentful and undervalued. Perhaps a better approach would be to have an open conversation about our expectations and responsibilities. I could express how I feel about the imbalance and suggest that we work together to find a solution where both of us contribute. This way, I'm not just refusing to help but actively working towards a healthier dynamic. In conclusion, while it might seem like I'm being AITA for refusing to help, it's more about setting boundaries to address an imbalance in our relationship. It's important to communicate my feelings and work together to find a fair solution rather than just stopping without discussion.
